ethics_check.report:

> In particular, the published harmonization study notes that MCI is generally not diagnosed in the Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) study. 6 For the CN-to-MCI analysis, participants were initially CN, with no earlier recorded MCI or AD diagnosis.

> CN and AD participants were in the same previously defined high-PRS interval (approximately 0.474-1.135) and were at least 75 years old at their last diagnostic assessment.

> In a separate genotyped population at high PRS and age 75 or older, 411 participants had normal cognition at their last diagnostic assessment and 751 had AD.

> Allowing intermediate MCI followed by CN also makes the interpretation of preserved cognition dependent on follow-up and outcome definition. 19, 20 In the separate older high-PRS population, CN participants had approximately one more year of education than participants with AD after covariate adjustment, including when diagnosis was confirmed at the final visit.

> Amyloid PET extended our earlier GRPa-PRS work 12 by showing that 56 of 97 selected high-PRS CN participants were amyloid-positive.

> All 893 participants were CN at prediction.

> All participants were CN at prediction.

report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("P < 0.05", "P < 0.05", "P ≥ 0.05", 
"P < 0.05", "P < 0.05", "P ≥ 0.05"), Text = c("Of the eight PRISM-AD tests across tasks, horizons and metrics, two reached nominal P < 0.05 and none met BH q < 0.05.", 
"Decile 6 reached nominal P < 0.05 but not BH q < 0.05.", "indicates nominal P ≥ 0.05.", 
"Ordinary stars denote BH q thresholds, . and (*) denotes nominal P < 0.05 with q above threshold.", 
"Ordinary *, ** and *** denote q < 0.05, 0.01 and 0.001. (*) denotes nominal P < 0.05 with q ≥ 0.05, and n.s. denotes nominal P ≥ 0.05.", 
"Ordinary *, ** and *** denote q < 0.05, 0.01 and 0.001. (*) denotes nominal P < 0.05 with q ≥ 0.05, and n.s. denotes nominal P ≥ 0.05."
)), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("P = 0.5968", "P = 0.4562", "P ≥ 0.05", "P ≥ 0.05"), Sentence = c("At three . years, the history-minus-current AP difference was -0.0080 (nominal P = 0.5968), and at five years it was -0.0105 (nominal P = 0.4562).", "At three . years, the history-minus-current AP difference was -0.0080 (nominal P = 0.5968), and at five years it was -0.0105 (nominal P = 0.4562).", "indicates nominal P ≥ 0.05.", "Ordinary *, ** and *** denote q < 0.05, 0.01 and 0.001. (*) denotes nominal P < 0.05 with q ≥ 0.05, and n.s. denotes nominal P ≥ 0.05." )), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

live_data_statements: In particular, the published harmonization study notes that MCI is generally not diagnosed in the Adult Changes in Thought (ACT) study. 6 For the CN-to-MCI analysis, participants were initially CN, with no earlier recorded MCI or AD diagnosis.
CN and AD participants were in the same previously defined high-PRS interval (approximately 0.474-1.135) and were at least 75 years old at their last diagnostic assessment.
In a separate genotyped population at high PRS and age 75 or older, 411 participants had normal cognition at their last diagnostic assessment and 751 had AD.

Allowing intermediate MCI followed by CN also makes the interpretation of preserved cognition dependent on follow-up and outcome definition. 19, 20 In the separate older high-PRS population, CN participants had approximately one more year of education than participants with AD after covariate adjustment, including when diagnosis was confirmed at the final visit.
Amyloid PET extended our earlier GRPa-PRS work 12 by showing that 56 of 97 selected high-PRS CN participants were amyloid-positive.
All 893 participants were CN at prediction.
Four participant-level, fold-adjusted HC3 omnibus F tests assessed C differences across PRS quintiles, with BH correction across the four groups (Supplementary Table 4).
All participants were CN at prediction.

text.text: Background: Older adults with high inherited Alzheimer's disease (AD) susceptibility can still be cognitively normal (CN).
An overall risk estimate alone does not show the cognitive and genetic contributions within a forecast.
Objective: To quantify clinical and genetic contributions to cognitive prognosis.
Methods: PRISM-AD combined nonlinear clinical functions and a polygenic risk score (PRS) term in 4,435 European-ancestry participants.
Participant-level internal validation evaluated first recorded mild cognitive impairment (MCI) after CN in 908 participants and AD dementia after MCI in 714, within three or five years.
Separately fitted comparators used identical inputs.
Post hoc clinical-course comparisons used regression with robust standard errors and Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction.
Results: PRISM-AD using current assessments achieved average precision of 0.2996 and 0.4094 for three-and five-year CN-to-MCI, with estimates close to logistic regression.
No PRISM-AD PRS increment met BH q < 0.05.
text.formatted: No PRISM-AD PRS increment met BH q < 0.05.

text.text: Three-year first-MCI forecasts characterized risk contributions in 893 initially CN participants.
A retrospective comparison over available follow-up included 95 participants with later AD and 701 with CN at their last diagnostic assessment.
Modeled genetic factors were higher in later AD in nine of ten shared cognitive-risk deciles.
After adjustment for modeled cognitive risk and fold, the genetic-factor ratio was 1.135 (nominal 95% CI, 1.073 to 1.201, BH q < 0.001).

text.text: Conclusions: Higher genetic contributions were associated with later AD at comparable modeled cognitive risk.
These exploratory profiles require independent validation before use in cognitive follow-up or prevention research.
Cognitively normal (CN) older adults vary in their risk of later impairment, motivating efforts to identify those who may warrant closer cognitive follow-up or evaluation for prevention research.

Clinical stage also defines the setting for Alzheimer's disease (AD) care: lecanemab slowed decline in early symptomatic AD, 1 while amyloid and tau biomarkers support biological diagnosis and blood-based assays improve pathology detection in symptomatic settings. 2, 3 Within this clinical course, forecasting first recorded mild cognitive impairment (MCI) after CN addresses the emergence of recognized impairment, whereas forecasting AD dementia after MCI addresses progression once impairment is present.
